unit.name: Physics: Particle Models and the Universe
unit.subtitle: How matter behaves, from gases to stress to the Big Bang.

lessons.title: Energy Transforming Matter — States and Heating
lessons.description: How heating changes state, internal energy and specific heat capacity.
lessons.content_html:
States of Matter and the Particle Model

All matter is made of tiny particles. The particle model helps explain how the same substance can exist as a solid, liquid or gas depending on how much energy its particles have.

In a solid, particles are held tightly in a regular lattice by strong forces of attraction. They vibrate but cannot move from place to place, which gives solids a fixed shape and volume. In a liquid, particles are still close together but the forces between them are weaker — they can slide past each other, so the liquid takes the shape of its container while keeping a definite volume. In a gas, particles are far apart and move rapidly in all directions, exerting pressure as they collide with the walls of their container.

Key Fact

Solid: particles vibrate in fixed positions — definite shape and volume. Liquid: particles slide past each other — definite volume, no fixed shape. Gas: particles move freely and rapidly — no fixed shape or volume, exerts pressure on its container.

Internal Energy

The internal energy of a substance is the sum of all the kinetic energy of its moving particles and all the potential energy stored in the forces between those particles. When you supply energy to a substance by heating it, the internal energy increases — the particles move faster or their arrangement changes, or both.

The temperature of a substance is a measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles. Raising the temperature means the particles are, on average, moving faster. However, during a change of state, temperature stays constant even though energy is still being supplied. This is because the energy goes into overcoming the forces between particles rather than speeding them up.

Specific Heat Capacity

Different materials need different amounts of energy to achieve the same temperature rise. Specific heat capacity (symbol \(c\)) is the quantity of energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. A high specific heat capacity means the substance stores a large amount of energy per kilogram for each degree of temperature rise.

The relationship between energy, mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change is:

$$\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta T$$

Where \(\Delta E\) is the change in internal energy in joules (J), \(m\) is the mass in kilograms (kg), \(c\) is the specific heat capacity in J/kg°C, and \(\Delta T\) is the temperature change in °C.

Worked example: An electric heater warms 2.0 kg of water from 20°C to 80°C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg°C. Calculate the energy transferred.

\(\Delta T = 80 - 20 = 60\)°C

\(\Delta E = 2.0 \times 4200 \times 60 = 504\,000\) J = 504 kJ

Always state the unit in your final answer. Check that all values are in SI units before substituting.

Key Fact

Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg°C — one of the highest of any common material. This means the sea absorbs large amounts of energy in summer and releases it slowly in winter, moderating coastal climates compared to inland areas.

Latent Heat

When a substance changes state, energy must be supplied (to melt or boil) or released (to freeze or condense) even though the temperature stays constant. This hidden energy is called latent heat. The word “latent” means hidden — the energy is used to break or form bonds between particles rather than raising the kinetic energy of particles.

There are two types: the specific latent heat of fusion (solid ↔ liquid) and the specific latent heat of vaporisation (liquid ↔ gas). The latent heat of vaporisation is always larger than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance, because changing from liquid to gas requires all the intermolecular forces to be overcome, not just weakened.

The energy for a change of state is calculated using:

$$E = m \times L$$

Where \(E\) is energy in joules, \(m\) is mass in kilograms, and \(L\) is the specific latent heat in J/kg.

Worked example: Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice. The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 334 000 J/kg.

\(E = 0.5 \times 334\,000 = 167\,000\) J = 167 kJ

To measure specific heat capacity in school, a known mass of material is heated electrically. Record the current, voltage, time and temperature rise: \(\Delta E = V \times I \times t\), then \(c = \Delta E \div (m \times \Delta T)\). Insulate the sample to reduce heat losses to the surroundings.

Key Fact

Energy for a change of state: \(E = mL\). During a change of state temperature remains constant — all energy goes into breaking or forming bonds between particles, not into changing their kinetic energy. Latent heat of vaporisation is always greater than latent heat of fusion.

Density and Changes of State

Density is mass divided by volume: \(\rho = m / V\). When a substance changes state, the mass is conserved but the volume usually changes — so the density changes too. Gases have much lower density than liquids because the particles are far apart. An important exception is water: ice is less dense than liquid water because the particles in ice form a structure that takes up slightly more space than liquid water particles, which is why ice floats.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In questions about heating curves, make sure you can explain why temperature stays flat during a change of state — the common error is to say “the substance is not gaining energy.” It is gaining energy; that energy is being used to break bonds between particles (latent heat), not raise temperature. In calculation questions, check whether the question asks for specific heat capacity (use \(\Delta E = mc\Delta T\)) or latent heat (use \(E = mL\)) — mixing them is the most common multi-step error.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The particle model explains the three states of matter: solids have particles in fixed positions; liquids allow sliding motion; gases have freely moving particles that exert pressure on their container.
  • Specific heat capacity (\(c\)) is the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1°C; use \(\Delta E = mc\Delta T\). Water’s high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg°C) makes it effective for thermal storage.
  • Latent heat (\(E = mL\)) is the energy for a change of state at constant temperature; the latent heat of vaporisation is always greater than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance.

practice_questions.text: Define specific heat capacity and explain why water is used as a coolant in car engines despite its relatively high cost compared with other fluids.
practice_questions.marks: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (1). Water's high specific heat capacity means it absorbs a large amount of energy per kilogram before its temperature rises significantly, making it effective at removing heat from the engine (1).

practice_questions.text: A 0.80 kg block of aluminium is heated electrically. The heater supplies 2.0 A at 12 V for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the expected temperature rise if no heat is lost to the surroundings. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/kg°C.
practice_questions.marks: Energy supplied: \(E = VIt = 12 \times 2.0 \times 300 = 7200\) J (1). Rearrange \(\Delta E = mc\Delta T\): \(\Delta T = \Delta E \div (mc) = 7200 \div (0.80 \times 900) = 7200 \div 720 = 10\)°C (1). Correct substitution with units shown (1). Final answer 10°C (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the particle model, why the temperature of water stays at 100°C while it is boiling, even though a heater is still supplying energy.
practice_questions.marks: At boiling point the supplied energy goes into breaking the forces of attraction between water molecules (1), allowing molecules to escape from the liquid and become gas particles (1). None of the energy goes into increasing the kinetic energy of the particles, so the temperature does not rise (1).

practice_questions.text: Calculate the energy needed to convert 0.25 kg of water at 100°C completely into steam at 100°C. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2 260 000 J/kg.
practice_questions.marks: \(E = mL = 0.25 \times 2\,260\,000 = 565\,000\) J (1). Unit correct: J or kJ stated (1).

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the specific heat capacity of water. She heats 0.50 kg of water using a 50 W immersion heater for 4.0 minutes and records a temperature rise of 11°C. Calculate the specific heat capacity from her results and suggest one reason why it differs from the accepted value of 4200 J/kg°C.
practice_questions.marks: Energy supplied: \(E = P \times t = 50 \times 240 = 12\,000\) J (1). \(c = E \div (m \times \Delta T) = 12\,000 \div (0.50 \times 11) = 12\,000 \div 5.5 \approx 2180\) J/kg°C (1). Calculated value is lower than accepted value (1). Reason: heat is lost to the surroundings / the container / the air, so not all energy goes into the water (1). Evaluation of experimental design — e.g. adding insulation or a lid would reduce heat loss (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how the density of water changes as it cools from liquid to solid (ice), and explain this behaviour using the particle model.
practice_questions.marks: Water's density increases as it cools from room temperature toward 4°C (1), but then decreases as it solidifies — ice is less dense than liquid water (1). In ice, water molecules form a more open crystalline structure with more space between them than in liquid water, so the same mass occupies a larger volume and density is lower (1).

It falls because energy is being absorbed

glossary_terms.definition: A scientific model describing matter as composed of tiny particles in constant motion, with properties depending on how closely packed and freely they move.
A state of matter in which particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement and can only vibrate about fixed positions.
A state of matter in which particles are close together but can slide past each other, giving a definite volume but no fixed shape.
A state of matter in which particles are far apart and move rapidly in random directions, filling any container they occupy.
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a substance.
A change from one physical state to another — for example, melting or boiling — that occurs at a fixed temperature.
The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a material by 1°C, measured in J/kg°C.
The energy required to change the state of a substance at constant temperature, without raising its temperature.
The energy per kilogram needed to melt a solid or freeze a liquid at constant temperature.
The energy per kilogram needed to boil a liquid or condense a gas at constant temperature.

lessons.title: Solids, Springs and Hooke's Law
lessons.description: How particles explain elasticity and stress in materials, including Hooke's law.
lessons.content_html:
Forces on Solid Materials

To stretch, bend or compress a solid object, you need to apply more than one force. A single force acting on an object simply accelerates it — it takes at least two forces, acting in opposite directions, to change its shape. Think of pulling both ends of a rubber band: one hand pulls left, the other pulls right, and the band stretches between them.

The particle model explains why this happens. In a solid, particles are held in place by forces of attraction and repulsion between neighbouring particles. Stretching the material pulls particles further apart, increasing the attractive forces. Compressing it pushes particles closer together, increasing the repulsive forces. When the external force is removed, these inter-particle forces can restore the original shape — if the material has not been overstretched.

Key Fact

Stretching, bending or compressing a solid requires two forces acting in opposite directions. The inter-particle forces in the solid resist the change in particle separation, which is the microscopic origin of the restoring force.

Elastic and Plastic Deformation

Elastic deformation occurs when a material springs back to its original shape once the force is removed. The inter-particle forces are strong enough to restore the original arrangement. A stretched spring or a stretched rubber band can both show elastic deformation.

Plastic deformation occurs when the force is large enough to permanently rearrange the particles. Particles slip past each other into new positions, and when the force is removed the material stays in its new deformed shape. Bending a metal paperclip until it stays bent is an example of plastic deformation. The particle model distinguishes these two types: elastic deformation keeps inter-particle spacings within the restoring-force range, while plastic deformation moves particles to entirely new equilibrium positions.

Hooke’s Law

Robert Hooke, working in the seventeenth century, discovered that for many springs and elastic materials, the extension is directly proportional to the applied force — provided the material is not stretched too far. This is now called Hooke’s law.

The mathematical form of Hooke’s law is:

$$F = k \times e$$

Where \(F\) is the force applied in newtons (N), \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m, and \(e\) is the extension in metres (m). A stiffer spring has a higher spring constant: it requires a larger force to produce the same extension.

Key Fact

Hooke’s law: \(F = ke\). On a force–extension graph the relationship is a straight line through the origin up to the limit of proportionality. Beyond this point the graph curves, and if the spring is permanently deformed it has exceeded its elastic limit.

Hang a spring from a clamp stand and measure its natural (unstretched) length with a ruler. Add known masses one at a time and record the new length each time. Calculate the extension by subtracting the natural length from the stretched length.

Plot force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis). The straight-line section through the origin shows Hooke’s law is obeyed; the gradient of this section equals the spring constant \(k\). When the line begins to curve upward, the limit of proportionality has been exceeded.

Worked example: A spring has a natural length of 15.0 cm. With a 200 g mass (weight ≈ 2.0 N) attached it stretches to 21.0 cm. Calculate the spring constant.

Extension: \(e = 21.0 - 15.0 = 6.0\) cm = 0.060 m. \(k = F \div e = 2.0 \div 0.060 \approx 33\) N/m.

Reduce parallax error when reading lengths by using a set square or a pointer at eye level. Always remove the loads gently after the experiment to check whether the spring has been permanently deformed.

Linear and Non-Linear Behaviour

Not all elastic materials show a linear (straight-line) force–extension relationship. A rubber band, for example, can stretch a great deal before the force rises sharply — its force–extension graph is a curve throughout, not a straight line at the start. Both the spring (linear up to its limit) and the rubber band (non-linear throughout) are elastic, because both return to their original shape, but only the spring obeys Hooke’s law in its initial range.

When work is done to stretch or compress a spring within its limit of proportionality, energy is stored as elastic potential energy. This can be recovered when the force is removed.

For a spring obeying Hooke’s law, the energy stored is:

$$E_e = \frac{1}{2} k e^2$$

Worked example: A spring with \(k = 50\) N/m is stretched by 0.10 m. Energy stored = \(\frac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 0.10^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 0.01 = 0.25\) J.

On a force–extension graph, the elastic potential energy equals the area under the straight-line section — a triangle with area \(\frac{1}{2} \times F \times e\), which is the same as \(\frac{1}{2} ke^2\) since \(F = ke\).

Key Fact

Elastic deformation: material returns to original shape; inter-particle forces restore the arrangement. Plastic deformation: particles slip permanently into new positions; the material does not recover. The boundary between them is the elastic limit of the material.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When using Hooke’s law, always check that the question says the spring is ‘within its limit of proportionality’ before applying \(F = ke\) — if the graph shows a curve, the equation does not apply. For the elastic potential energy equation \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\), ensure the extension is in metres and the spring constant is in N/m. A common error is to halve the force rather than the whole expression — write out every step of the substitution.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stretching, compressing or bending a solid requires two forces in opposite directions; the inter-particle forces provide a restoring force when the deforming forces are removed.
  • Hooke’s law states \(F = ke\): extension is proportional to force up to the limit of proportionality, giving a straight-line graph through the origin with gradient \(k\).
  • Elastic deformation is reversible; plastic deformation is permanent. Elastic potential energy \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\) is stored in a stretched spring and can be fully recovered if the elastic limit is not exceeded.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the particle model, why a steel spring returns to its original length after being stretched within its elastic limit, but does not return to its original length if it is stretched too far.
practice_questions.marks: Within the elastic limit, particles are displaced from their equilibrium positions but inter-particle forces are strong enough to pull them back when the load is removed (1). If stretched too far, particles slip past each other into new positions (1); the forces between them in these new positions do not restore the original arrangement, so the spring is permanently deformed (1).

practice_questions.text: A spring is hung vertically. A 0.30 kg mass is attached and the spring extends by 6.0 cm. Calculate the spring constant. (Use g = 10 N/kg.)

A student investigates the force–extension relationship of a spring. Describe the apparatus you would use and the measurements you would take to determine whether the spring obeys Hooke's law and to find its spring constant.
practice_questions.marks: Apparatus: spring attached to clamp stand, ruler fixed vertically alongside, known masses (1). Measure natural length; add masses one at a time and record length each time; calculate extension (1). Independent variable: force (mass × g); dependent variable: extension; control variable: same spring throughout (1). Plot force (y) against extension (x); if straight line through origin, Hooke's law obeyed; gradient = spring constant (1).

practice_questions.text: A spring with spring constant 80 N/m is compressed by 5.0 cm. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored.
practice_questions.marks: \(E_e = \frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 0.05^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 0.0025 = 0.10\) J (1). Unit: J stated (1).

practice_questions.text: The force–extension graph for a spring shows a straight line from 0 to 0.12 m extension (at 6 N), then curves upward. Identify the spring constant and the force at the limit of proportionality. Then explain what would happen to the spring if a 10 N load were applied and removed.
practice_questions.marks: Spring constant: gradient of linear section = 6 ÷ 0.12 = 50 N/m (1). Limit of proportionality: 6 N at 0.12 m extension (1). At 10 N the spring is beyond its limit of proportionality (1) — the relationship is no longer linear (1). After removing the 10 N load, the spring may not return to its original length — it could be permanently deformed beyond its elastic limit (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the force–extension behaviour of a steel spring and a rubber band when a gradually increasing force is applied, and then removed.
practice_questions.marks: Steel spring: linear force–extension relationship up to limit of proportionality (Hooke's law obeyed) (1); returns to original length when force removed, provided elastic limit not exceeded (elastic deformation) (1). Rubber band: non-linear relationship throughout — the graph curves (1); also returns to original length when force removed (elastic), but different extension on loading and unloading (hysteresis) (1).

glossary_terms.definition: A model of matter in which particles are held in fixed positions in solids by forces between them; applying external forces changes particle separation and deforms the material.
The increase in the length of a spring or elastic material when a force is applied, equal to the stretched length minus the natural length.
The principle that extension is proportional to force for a spring or other elastic object, as long as the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
A measure of the stiffness of a spring or elastic object, equal to force divided by extension, measured in N/m.
The maximum force up to which a spring or material obeys Hooke's law; beyond this the force–extension graph curves.
Deformation in which the material returns to its original shape and size when the applied force is removed.
Deformation in which the material does not return to its original shape after the applied force is removed; the change is permanent.
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object that has not been deformed beyond its elastic limit.

lessons.title: Gases, Pressure and Fluids
lessons.description: Why gas pressure changes when you compress or heat it, plus pressure in liquids.
lessons.content_html:
Gas Pressure and the Particle Model

A gas exerts gas pressure on any surface it is in contact with. The particle model explains why: gas particles are in constant, rapid, random motion. When they collide with the walls of a container, each collision exerts a tiny force on the wall. The total pressure is the combined effect of billions of these collisions per second.

If the volume of the container is reduced at constant temperature, the particles are confined to a smaller space. They travel shorter distances between collisions with the walls, so they hit the walls more frequently. More collisions per second means a greater pressure. Conversely, increasing the volume at constant temperature reduces the collision frequency and lowers the pressure.

Key Fact

Gas pressure is caused by particle collisions with container walls. Decreasing the volume (at constant temperature) increases the frequency of collisions and therefore increases the pressure. Increasing the volume decreases pressure.

Boyle’s Law

Robert Boyle, working in the 1660s, measured the relationship between pressure and volume for a trapped gas at constant temperature. He found that pressure and volume are inversely proportional: as one doubles, the other halves. This is now known as Boyle’s law.

The mathematical form is:

$$p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2$$

Where \(p_1\) and \(V_1\) are the initial pressure and volume, and \(p_2\) and \(V_2\) are the final pressure and volume. Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa) and volume in cubic metres (m³). Boyle’s law applies only when temperature and the amount of gas are kept constant.

A gas occupies 0.60 m³ at a pressure of 200 kPa. The gas is compressed at constant temperature until its volume is 0.20 m³. Calculate the new pressure.

Using \(p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\):

\(p_2 = \frac{p_1 V_1}{V_2} = \frac{200 \times 0.60}{0.20} = \frac{120}{0.20} = 600\) kPa

Always check units are consistent before substituting. Pressure can be in Pa or kPa as long as both \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) use the same unit.

Absolute Zero

Temperature affects gas pressure too. Raising the temperature of a gas at constant volume gives the particles more kinetic energy — they move faster and collide with the walls more forcefully and more frequently, so pressure increases. Cooling the gas has the opposite effect. Scientists found that extrapolating the pressure–temperature relationship for any gas reaches zero pressure at the same temperature: −273°C. This is called absolute zero.

The Kelvin scale uses absolute zero as its starting point (0 K). To convert: \(T(K) = T(°C) + 273\). The Kelvin scale is important for gas law calculations because pressure and volume are proportional to temperature in kelvin, not in Celsius.

Key Fact

Absolute zero = −273°C = 0 K. At absolute zero, particles would have minimum possible kinetic energy. To convert to kelvin: add 273. Gas pressure and volume are proportional to temperature in kelvin.

Pressure in Fluids

A fluid (liquid or gas) exerts pressure at right angles (normal) to any surface it is in contact with. This pressure acts equally in all directions at a given depth. The equation for pressure on a solid surface is:

$$P = \frac{F}{A}$$

Where \(P\) is pressure in pascals (Pa), \(F\) is the force in newtons (N), and \(A\) is the area in square metres (m²). One pascal equals one newton per square metre.

Pressure in a liquid increases with depth because there is a greater weight of liquid above. The pressure also depends on the density of the liquid. The equation for pressure due to a column of liquid is:

$$P = \rho g h$$

Where \(\rho\) (rho) is the density of the liquid in kg/m³, \(g\) is gravitational field strength (approximately 10 N/kg near Earth’s surface), and \(h\) is the depth in metres.

Because pressure increases with depth, the upward force on the bottom surface of a submerged object is greater than the downward force on its top surface. This net upward force is called upthrust. An object floats when the upthrust equals its weight. An object sinks when its weight exceeds the upthrust. Whether an object floats or sinks depends on the relationship between its density and the density of the fluid: an object denser than the fluid sinks; one less dense than the fluid floats.

Worked example: Calculate the pressure at 5.0 m depth in sea water (density 1025 kg/m³). \(P = 1025 \times 10 \times 5.0 = 51\,250\) Pa ≈ 51 kPa (plus atmospheric pressure above the water surface).

Atmospheric Pressure

Earth’s atmosphere is a layer of gas held around the planet by gravity. The atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately 100 000 Pa (100 kPa). Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude because there is less air above — fewer particle collisions occur from the thinner air overhead.

Key Fact

Pressure at depth \(h\) in a fluid: \(P = \rho g h\). Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude because the column of air above is shorter and less dense, so fewer particle collisions occur per unit area.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When applying Boyle’s law \(p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\), check that temperature is stated as constant — the law does not apply if temperature changes. For pressure-at-depth calculations using \(P = \rho g h\), remember that \(h\) is the depth below the surface, not the total height of the container. Exam questions sometimes give data in cm³ or litres — always convert to m³ before substituting. Also, do not confuse gas pressure (from \(P = F/A\)) with liquid pressure (from \(P = \rho g h\)) — identify which formula the context demands before writing.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Gas pressure is caused by particle collisions with container walls. Boyle’s law: \(p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\) at constant temperature — decreasing volume increases pressure proportionally.
  • Absolute zero (−273°C = 0 K) is the temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy. The Kelvin scale is required for proportional gas-law calculations.
  • Pressure in a liquid increases with depth: \(P = \rho g h\). Upthrust arises because the deeper surface of a submerged object experiences greater pressure than the upper surface. Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude.

practice_questions.text: A bicycle tyre contains air at 300 kPa in a volume of 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³. The air is compressed at constant temperature to a volume of 0.8 × 10⁻³ m³. Calculate the new pressure.
Explain, using the particle model, why the pressure of a gas in a sealed container increases when the container is heated at constant volume.
practice_questions.marks: Heating increases the kinetic energy of gas particles (1), so they move faster and collide with the container walls more frequently and with greater force (1), producing a greater pressure per unit area (1).

practice_questions.text: A diver descends to a depth of 20 m in fresh water (density 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg). Calculate the pressure due to the water at this depth.
practice_questions.marks: P = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 20 = 200 000 Pa = 200 kPa (1). Unit stated correctly (1).

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by absolute zero and explain why a temperature scale based on absolute zero is more useful for gas-law calculations than the Celsius scale.
practice_questions.marks: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature (−273°C or 0 K) at which particles have minimum kinetic energy / gas pressure would reach zero (1). On the Kelvin scale, temperature starts at absolute zero, so all Kelvin values are positive (1). Gas pressure and volume are directly proportional to temperature in kelvin (1); using Celsius would give incorrect ratios because the Celsius zero is arbitrary, not the true minimum of thermal energy (1).

practice_questions.text: A submarine has a flat circular hatch of radius 0.40 m. The hatch is at a depth where the water pressure is 5.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the force exerted on the hatch by the water, and evaluate whether a human could open the hatch by pushing from the inside at this depth. (Atmospheric pressure inside the submarine = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.)
practice_questions.marks: Area of hatch: A = π × 0.40² ≈ 0.503 m² (1). Net pressure difference on hatch = (5.0 − 1.0) × 10⁵ = 4.0 × 10⁵ Pa (1). Force = P × A = 4.0 × 10⁵ × 0.503 ≈ 201 000 N ≈ 200 kN (1). A typical human can exert around 500–1000 N pushing force (1). 200 000 N far exceeds human capability — the hatch could not be opened by hand; mechanical assistance or pressure equalisation would be needed (1).

practice_questions.text: A gas at 200 kPa occupies 0.30 m³. Describe what must be done to the gas to reduce its pressure to 100 kPa, and calculate the new volume required, assuming temperature does not change.
practice_questions.marks: To reduce pressure, the volume must be increased (1) — expanding the gas at constant temperature reduces particle collision frequency with the walls (1). New volume: V₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ p₂ = (200 × 0.30) ÷ 100 = 60 ÷ 100 = 0.60 m³ (1). Unit m³ stated (1).

knowledge_checks.q: What causes the pressure exerted by a gas on its container walls?
options: The weight of the gas pressing downward
The expansion of the gas outward

Match each term to its correct description.
right: Pressure exerted by the weight of air at sea level (~100 kPa)
Net upward force on a submerged object from increasing pressure with depth

glossary_terms.definition: A force per unit area exerted by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container, measured in pascals (Pa).
For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant; as pressure increases, volume decreases proportionally.
The lowest possible temperature, −273°C or 0 K, at which particles have minimum possible kinetic energy and gas pressure would reach zero.
A temperature scale starting at absolute zero (0 K = −273°C), where a change of 1 K equals a change of 1°C.
Any substance that can flow — both liquids and gases are fluids.
The net upward force exerted by a fluid on a submerged or partially submerged object, caused by the greater pressure at greater depth.
The pressure exerted by the weight of the atmosphere above a surface, approximately 100 000 Pa at sea level.

lessons.title: Stars, Galaxies and the Big Bang
lessons.description: How models help us understand a universe far older than us. Key concepts and applications explained.
lessons.content_html:
Our Solar System and Beyond

The solar system consists of the Sun and all the objects gravitationally bound to it — the eight planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), their moons, and countless smaller bodies such as asteroids and comets. The planets orbit the Sun in nearly circular paths, all in the same direction. Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps them in orbit — the gravitational pull continuously changes the direction of each planet's velocity, keeping it in a circular path without changing its speed.

Our solar system sits within the galaxy called the Milky Way. The universe contains billions of galaxies, each containing hundreds of millions to hundreds of billions of stars. On this scale, distances are so vast that light — travelling at roughly 300 000 km per second — takes years, millennia, or even billions of years to cross them.

Key Fact

Planets orbit the Sun in (almost) circular paths because gravity provides a centripetal force. An object in a circular orbit moves at constant speed but changing velocity — its direction changes continuously, so velocity changes even though speed does not. For a stable orbit, if the orbital speed changes, the radius of the orbit must also change. The further a planet is from the Sun, the slower its orbital speed and the longer its year.

The Life Cycle of a Star

Stars form from vast clouds of gas (mainly hydrogen) and dust. Gravity pulls the cloud inward: as the gas is compressed, work is done on it, and the particle model predicts the temperature rises (compressed gas gets hotter because the particles collide more forcefully as they are pushed closer together). When the core temperature rises sufficiently, hydrogen nuclei gain enough kinetic energy to overcome their electrostatic repulsion and undergo nuclear fusion — fusing into helium nuclei and releasing enormous energy.

This energy release creates an outward radiation pressure that balances the inward gravitational collapse. A star in this stable phase — like our Sun — is called a main sequence star. Our Sun has been on the main sequence for roughly 4.6 billion years and is expected to remain there for a similar period.

When a star’s hydrogen fuel runs low, fusion can no longer balance gravity. The core contracts and heats further, causing the outer layers to expand dramatically. The star becomes a red giant (for a star like the Sun) or a red supergiant (for a much more massive star).

A star like the Sun eventually sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving behind a dense, hot remnant called a white dwarf, which slowly cools over billions of years.

A much more massive star ends its life more violently. Fusion in a massive star’s core builds up progressively heavier elements until iron is reached — iron cannot release energy by fusion. The core then collapses catastrophically and the outer layers are expelled in a supernova explosion. The remnant may become a neutron star or a black hole.

Red-Shift and the Expanding Universe

When astronomers examine light from distant galaxies, they find that the dark absorption lines in the spectrum are shifted towards longer, redder wavelengths compared to the same lines measured in a laboratory. This phenomenon is called red-shift. It arises because the galaxy is moving away from us: as light travels through expanding space, its wavelength is stretched.

A key observation is that more distant galaxies show a greater red-shift — they are moving away from us faster. This pattern holds in every direction, which means the universe as a whole is expanding: space itself is growing, carrying galaxies apart with it. Scientists use this relationship between distance and recession speed as evidence for the expanding universe model.

Key Fact

Red-shift: light from receding galaxies is stretched to longer (redder) wavelengths. More distant galaxies have greater red-shift, meaning they are moving away faster. This is evidence that the universe is expanding.

The Big Bang Model (IaS3 — Scientific Models)

If the universe is currently expanding, then tracing back in time suggests it was once much smaller, hotter and denser. The scientific explanation for the origin of the universe is the Big Bang model. According to this model, the universe began roughly 14 billion years ago in a state of extreme temperature and density, and has been expanding and cooling ever since.

The acceptance of the Big Bang model is a good example of how scientific models develop as evidence accumulates (IaS3). When Edwin Hubble published his observations of galactic red-shifts in 1929, showing that galaxies were receding at speeds proportional to their distance, it provided the first strong observational support for an expanding universe. The model became far more secure in 1965 when Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detected a faint microwave glow coming uniformly from all directions in the sky — the cosmic microwave background (CMB). This radiation is interpreted as the cooled remnant of the intense heat of the early universe.

Over the last century, telescope technology has improved dramatically. Ground-based observatories can detect visible light from billions of light-years away. Space-based telescopes can observe in wavelength ranges — infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray, microwave — blocked by Earth’s atmosphere. Removing the atmosphere also eliminates atmospheric blurring, allowing much finer detail to be resolved.

Each new generation of observational data has refined our picture of the early universe, the large-scale structure of galaxies, and the expansion rate. These improved data have consistently supported and strengthened the Big Bang model, rather than overturning it — illustrating how accumulating evidence increases scientific confidence in a model (IaS3).

Key Fact

Two key pieces of evidence for the Big Bang: (1) Hubble’s 1929 observations showing that galactic recession speed increases with distance — red-shift evidence for an expanding universe. (2) Penzias and Wilson’s 1965 detection of the cosmic microwave background — the cooled remnant of radiation from the early universe.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In ‘explain’ questions about red-shift, always state two things: what red-shift means (wavelength of light is increased / shifted to longer wavelengths) AND what it implies about the galaxy’s motion (moving away from us). Saying “the galaxy is moving away” without explaining the wavelength change scores only partial credit. For Big Bang model questions, you may be asked to evaluate the model as evidence accumulates — frame your answer using the language of IaS3: “each new observation either supports or challenges the model; the model gains confidence when predictions are confirmed by independent data.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stars form from collapsing gas clouds; nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in the core provides energy that balances gravitational collapse during the main sequence. Massive stars end as supernovae; Sun-like stars become red giants then white dwarfs.
  • Red-shift — the stretching of wavelengths from receding galaxies — shows that more distant galaxies move away faster, evidence that the universe is expanding.
  • The Big Bang model explains the expanding universe as originating from an extremely hot, dense state roughly 14 billion years ago. The cosmic microwave background (detected 1965) and galactic red-shifts (Hubble, 1929) are its two main observational pillars.

practice_questions.text: Explain what red-shift is, and describe how observations of red-shift from distant galaxies support the Big Bang model.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Red-shift is the increase in observed wavelength (shift towards the red end of the spectrum) of light from a galaxy moving away from us (1). More distant galaxies show greater red-shift, meaning they are receding faster (1). This pattern applies in all directions (1). Running the expansion backward in time suggests the universe was once much smaller, hotter and denser (1). This is consistent with the Big Bang model — the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding ever since (1). The cosmic microwave background provides independent supporting evidence — a faint microwave glow from all directions, interpreted as cooled remnant radiation from the early universe (1). Secure: Four or five valid points with a clear logical link. Developing: Describes red-shift and expanding universe but does not link them explicitly to Big Bang. Emerging: Names red-shift without explaining its significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe the sequence of events in the formation of a star from a cloud of gas and dust, up to the point at which it becomes a stable main sequence star.
practice_questions.marks: Gravity pulls gas cloud together (1). As gas is compressed, its temperature rises (work is done on it by compression) (1). When core temperature is high enough, nuclear fusion of hydrogen begins; outward radiation pressure balances gravitational collapse and the star becomes stable (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why an object moving in a circular orbit has a constantly changing velocity even if its speed does not change.
practice_questions.marks: Velocity is a vector — it has both magnitude (speed) and direction (1). In circular orbit the direction of motion changes continuously, so velocity changes even though speed (the magnitude) remains constant (1).

practice_questions.text: The light from a distant galaxy shows that a particular spectral line has a wavelength of 520 nm. The same line measured in the laboratory has a wavelength of 500 nm. State whether this galaxy is moving towards or away from Earth, and justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Moving away from Earth (1). The observed wavelength (520 nm) is longer than the laboratory value (500 nm) — this is red-shift, indicating the galaxy is receding (1).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how increasing improvements in telescope technology over the last 100 years have affected scientific confidence in the Big Bang model, using the concept of scientific models and evidence.
practice_questions.marks: Improved telescopes allow detection of fainter, more distant galaxies (1). Observations at wavelengths beyond visible light (e.g. microwave for CMB, infrared, X-ray) are possible from space without atmospheric interference (1). Each new dataset either supports or challenges the Big Bang model; repeated independent confirmation increases confidence (IaS3) (1). For example, refined measurements of the CMB by satellite missions have confirmed its temperature and uniformity to high precision, matching Big Bang predictions (1). No major observations have overturned the model; instead they have added detail (e.g. dark energy driving accelerated expansion) — illustrating that scientific models evolve but are not abandoned lightly when evidence is inconsistent (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the eventual fate of a star similar in mass to the Sun with the eventual fate of a star much more massive than the Sun.
practice_questions.marks: Sun-like star: expands into a red giant as hydrogen runs low (1); sheds outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a cooling white dwarf (1). Massive star: also expands (red supergiant), but core collapses catastrophically once iron accumulates (1); outer layers explode as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole (1).

glossary_terms.definition: The Sun and all the objects gravitationally bound to it, including eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets.
A gravitationally bound system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter. Galaxies range enormously in size — the Milky Way contains roughly 100–400 billion stars.
The joining of two light atomic nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing large amounts of energy.
A star in the stable phase of its life cycle, during which it fuses hydrogen into helium in its core, producing energy that balances gravitational collapse.
A stage in stellar evolution in which a star has exhausted its core hydrogen and expanded to many times its original size, with a cooler, red outer surface.
An explosive stellar event in which a massive star's core collapses and its outer layers are violently expelled, briefly outshining entire galaxies.
An increase in the observed wavelength of light from a source that is moving away from the observer; the further a galaxy is, the greater its red-shift.
The scientific model proposing that the universe began from an extremely hot, dense state approximately 14 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.
Faint microwave radiation detected uniformly in all directions, interpreted as the cooled remnant of radiation from the early, extremely hot universe shortly after the Big Bang.
